1.pericope_label: Publicans draw near to hear him; Pharisees and scribes murmur that he receives sinners and eats with them

schools.summary: Gill sets the scene on a sabbath as Jesus leaves the Pharisee’s house, the crowd closing in once he is outside.

Henry defends the publicans as put into an ill name by national prejudice, notes the modesty of a crowd that came only near enough to hear, and observes that the meal was attacked because the preaching could not be.

Ellicott dates the boldness of the approach to Christ’s withdrawal from the Pharisee’s table; Robertson parses the periphrastic imperfect, the purpose infinitive, the doubled article separating publicans from sinners, the sneering demonstrative and the settled present of a habitual welcome; Barnes exposes the inference that kindness proves shared character.

Clarke reads the pair as tax-gatherers and heathens and presses the welcoming verb as taking to the bosom; Wesley limits “all” to all who were in that place and puts the scene in Galilee of the Gentiles.
Ambrose reads the chapter as the remedy offered after the fall; Gregory contrasts true justice, which feels compassion, with false justice, which scorns.

debates: Whether the “sinners” are lax Jews or Gentiles: Clarke calls them heathens who believed neither in Christ nor Moses, and Wesley and Henry suspect a setting in Galilee of the Gentiles, while the grammarians treat them simply as the disreputable of the district.
outliers: Robertson reaches outside the text for a comparison, likening the outcasts to the untouchables of India.

3.pericope_label: The parable of the lost sheep: the shepherd leaves the ninety and nine, seeks the one, carries it home and calls for shared joy

schools.summary: Gill takes the parable to convict the Pharisees, encourage the publicans and vindicate the speaker at once.

Clarke supplies the natural history of a straying sheep and the raven that blinds the lamb, and asks who but a Pharisee or a devil would fault the rescue; Wesley identifies the wilderness as common land and reads the three parables as one answer.

Robertson makes the wilderness ordinary pasture rather than peril, reads the seeking as a linear present closed by an effective aorist, and hears fellowship demanded by the verb of shared joy; Lightfoot documents the Jewish habit of dividing between one and ninety-nine; Ellicott allows both a narrow application to one soul present and a cosmic one in which the ninety and nine are unfallen creatures elsewhere.
Cyril presses the perfection of the number ten times ten and denies that the shepherd was angry with the rest, who were left in safety.
Gregory of Nyssa observes that the sheep was neither punished nor driven but lifted and carried gently.

Gregory takes the ninety and nine for the angelic companies left in heaven and dwells on the call to rejoice with the shepherd rather than with the sheep; Augustine dissents, reading them as the proud who want to appear alone; Ambrose calls the shepherd rich, of whom each of us is a hundredth part.

debates: What the ninety and nine stand for. Ellicott and Gregory read unfallen angels, Clarke the whole flock of mankind, Robertson simply sheep at their usual pasture, while Augustine reverses the picture entirely and finds in them the proud who lack the unity that would complete them.
outliers: Clarke argues from his own observation of sheep and of ravens blinding lambs rather than from the text.

7.pericope_label: Joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons which need no repentance

schools.summary: Gill allows the heaven in view to be either the church below or the angelic heaven above.

Barnes strips the added word “persons”, allows the just ones to be angels, denies any sinless men on earth and forbids reading the numbers as a ratio; Ellicott hears an indignant protest veiled as concession against Pharisaic self-righteousness; Robertson finds no comparative in the Greek and takes the concession as argumentative, condemning the critics from their own claims; Lightfoot documents “just persons” as the ordinary Jewish name for the finally saved.

Clarke lets the phrase describe genuinely upright people who cannot repent of sins they never committed, instances Cornelius, and reports without rejecting the view that the ninety and nine are angels; Wesley calls the joy solemn and festal, beginning in Christ and spreading to angels and the spirits of just men.
Cyril of Jerusalem applies the verse directly to catechumens, urging a new heart so that heaven may be glad.
Tertullian roots the joy in ownership: the seeker is the loser, the loser the owner, so the gladness is the Creator’s.

debates: Who the ninety and nine just persons are. Barnes leaves the term open to angels and denies any sinless men; Clarke defends a real class of upright people and passes on the angelic reading as worth weighing; Ellicott and Robertson deny the concession altogether and read it as irony aimed at the Pharisees.
outliers: Clarke argues from a general maxim about unexpected advantages rather than from the passage, and Lightfoot digresses into rabbinic play on the two forms of a Hebrew letter.

8.pericope_label: The parable of the lost coin: the woman lights a candle, sweeps and seeks until she finds it, and joy arises before the angels of God

schools.summary: Gill makes the woman Christ and the coins the Jewish nation, and presses the coin’s helplessness as proof of the sinner’s passivity in conversion; Calvin explains the greater joy as the brighter shining of mercy on one already cut off, ascribed to God after the manner of men.

Ellicott finds significance in a coin lost indoors and in a woman seeking, and refuses to reduce the change of sex to an appeal to the women listening; Robertson traces the coin’s name to a verb for grasping, infers a windowless house with a dirt floor, and observes that she lost the coin whereas the shepherd did not lose the sheep; Barnes notes the sum was small but was all she had; Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic parallel of candles lit for a lost shekel.
Clarke keeps the ancient coin names and observes that a coin long lost loses colour, gathers dirt and may have its image worn away, while warning that parables must not be made to go on all fours.

Chrysostom reads the coin as man struck with the royal image, complementing the sheep; Gregory of Nyssa relocates the search inside one soul, the coins being the virtues and the house the conscience; Gregory Nazianzen makes the heavenly powers partners in the joy, and Theophylact ranks friends against nearer neighbours.
Gregory makes the woman God and the nine coins the nine angelic orders, man created tenth; Augustine reads the nine instead as those who prefer themselves to returning sinners.

debates: What the nine remaining coins are. Gregory counts nine angelic orders with man as the tenth; Augustine takes them for the self-satisfied; Gill identifies them with the scribes and Pharisees; Gregory of Nyssa makes them the other virtues of a single soul.
Who the woman is: Christ for Gill, God and the wisdom of God for Gregory, and for Ellicott partly the Wisdom of Proverbs and partly the church.
outliers: Clarke argues from the physical decay of a mislaid coin rather than from the text, and Robertson reconstructs the house from archaeology to explain the lamp.

11.pericope_label: A certain man had two sons; the younger asks for his portion of goods, and the father divides his living between them

schools.summary: Calvin reads the parable as confirming the preceding doctrine, with a father who goes out to meet rather than merely pardon; Gill takes the younger son for the elect among publicans and sinners.
Henry makes God father to the whole family of Adam, so that the publicans are the Pharisees’ own brethren, and draws the sons as characters rather than ciphers.

Lightfoot finds the Jew-and-Gentile reading long established and fitting; Ellicott holds the narrow and wide applications together but turns the elder son against the angelic reading of the ninety and nine; Barnes and Robertson work out the law of the double share, the younger taking a third and probably in movable goods, with Roman and Syrophoenician parallels for claiming it early.
Clarke calls the early division an immemorial eastern custom the father could not legally refuse, framed to protect a child from ill usage.

Cyril reports and rejects the Israel-and-Gentiles reading on the ground that the elder son’s boast cannot fit a people so often reproved, preferring two ranks of the righteous, and locates free will in the father’s refusal either to detain or to drive out.

Ambrose reads the three parables as pity, intercession and reconciliation; Augustine finds two nations from the beginning of the race, one keeping the worship of God and one deserting to idols, and hears in the request a soul pleased with its own power asking for what was always a gift.

Chrysostom distinguishes a sheep that cannot find its way back from a son who acts by his own will, and refuses the reading that makes the elder son the angels; Theophylact makes the substance the capacity of reason with its liberty, together with heaven, earth, the Law and the Prophets; Basil notes that age is a matter of mind rather than grey hairs.

debates: Whom the two sons represent. Barnes, Henry and Ellicott read Pharisees and publicans, with Lightfoot and Ellicott extending it to Jew and Gentile; Augustine sees two nations from the creation of the race; Cyril rejects the national reading because the elder son’s claim of unbroken obedience cannot be said of Israel, and substitutes two ranks of the righteous; Chrysostom reports and rejects an older view that the elder son is the angels.

Ellicott argues from the elder son back to the earlier parables, holding that because he cannot stand for unfallen creation the ninety and nine sheep and the nine coins should not be read as angels either — against the reading he himself had allowed on verse 4.
outliers: Clarke supports the legal point from an eastern law code and its scale of fines rather than from Jewish sources.

13.pericope_label: The younger son gathers all, journeys into a far country, wastes his substance in riotous living, and a mighty famine leaves him in want

schools.summary: Gill argues that sin strips the man of the divine image and of all strength for good, leaving nothing of free will and no capacity to prepare for conversion.

Robertson sets the gathering against a scattering that is the word for winnowing and derives “riotous” from a root meaning unsaveable; Ellicott fills in the emigration to Alexandria, Rome or Corinth and reads the far country as a spirit wandering from God, with the famine under Claudius behind the second verse; Barnes keeps to the surface, converting the property to money and naturalising the famine from crop failure and plague.

Clarke supplies a motive of flight from legal penalty and reproach, traces the money to harlots on the elder brother’s later charge, and supposes a country of riot where want must follow; Wesley compresses it to a God not in all his thoughts and grace squandered.

Augustine traces the departure to a perverse imitation of God’s ungoverned freedom, ending in a soul grown cold and vanishing from truth, and defines prodigal living as outward display that exhausts a man within; Ambrose calls the famine a fast not of food but of good works.
Chrysostom denies that the far country is a place at all, since God is everywhere present; the flight is of the heart, so as to stand at a distance.

debates: Whether the prodigal answers to the stubborn and rebellious son of Deuteronomy. Lightfoot raises the question and denies it, showing from the Sanhedrin’s own definition that the conditions are drawn so narrowly that hardly such a son could exist.
outliers: Clarke infers a flight from legal penalty that the narrative does not mention, and Lightfoot breaks off into an anecdote about an emperor’s appetite.

15.pericope_label: He joins himself to a citizen of that country, is sent into the fields to feed swine, and no man gives him even the husks

schools.summary: Gill rejects both saints and devil — the devil being the country’s prince rather than a citizen — and identifies an unregenerate legal preacher with gifts but no grace.

Robertson reads the passive of a verb meaning to glue and derives the pod’s name from the word for horn; Ellicott hears in the same verb the cleaving of husband to wife, denies that the citizen can be the tempter since he is one of many and serves to punish and preserve rather than to seduce, and records the manuscript variant behind the coarser phrase; Barnes takes the citizen simply for a landowner and quotes a traveller on the carob pods still fed to swine.

Wesley makes the citizen the devil or one of his children; Clarke argues from a botanist that the word never meant husks, and reports the Egyptian swineherd’s exclusion from society, worship and marriage.
Ambrose calls the citizen a prince of the world and the farm an enslavement to worldly goods, and Bede glosses the farm the same way; Augustine names a prince of the air.
Theophylact assigns the feeding of swine to those who outdid others in vice and taught their trade to others.

debates: Whom the citizen represents. Wesley, Ambrose, Bede and Augustine make him the devil or a prince of this world; Gill argues the devil is that country’s ruler and not one of its citizens, and proposes a graceless legal preacher; Ellicott rules out the tempter because the citizen is one of many and functions to punish rather than to seduce, and reads him as worldly prudence and religionless ethics.
Whether the word rendered husks means husks at all: Clarke denies it on botanical authority, and Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott all identify the carob pod instead.
outliers: Barnes and Clarke both settle the botany from outside sources, a travel narrative and a seventeenth-century naturalist, rather than from the text.

17.pericope_label: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger

schools.summary: Gill divides the madness between the voluptuary and the self-righteous man; Calvin makes hunger the best teacher and God’s wedges hard for hard knots, but insists that hope of the father’s kindness is what gave courage, so repentance must begin in an acknowledgment of mercy.
Henry treats the coming to oneself as the turning point of conversion, where the convinced sinner sees the meanest servant of God happier than himself.

Barnes reads the phrase as recovery from derangement and hears the sting in a son who had property and a kind father; Robertson keeps it spatial and weighs the Greek clause against clause, loaves like a flood against a man perishing here; Ellicott distinguishes the false self the man had been living to, and identifies the hired servants as those who serve for reward yet find enough.
Clarke calls sin a course of madness and repentance a return to sound sense, and records the added “here” in many witnesses.

Basil sorts obedience into servile, mercenary and filial; Chrysostom hears wounded rank, a free and noble son sunk below hirelings by his own will; Gregory of Nyssa marks the arc from contempt to a chastened return.

Ambrose turns the phrase into a paradox, that returning to God restores a man to himself, and gives the heir’s right against the wage; Augustine locates the turn in conscience and sharpens the mercenaries into preachers who work for a temporal reward; Bede notes the son asks only a hireling’s place and admits he could not deserve even that.

debates: What the hired servants stand for. Ellicott and Basil read them as a real if lower order of obedience that is genuinely fed; Augustine narrows them to preachers of the true word who work for pay; Ambrose contrasts them with the heir who holds the pledge of the Spirit.
outliers: Calvin generalises from the parable into a doctrine of affliction as God’s ordinary teaching method, well beyond the scope of the verse.

18.pericope_label: I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes leaving one’s vices while remaining in the far country from leaving the country itself, its acquaintance and its ministry.

Robertson makes the resolve an act of will after clear sight and notes the hard word said first, a verb for missing the mark; Ellicott presses the aorist back to the first act of sin and reads the willingness to be a hired servant as the contrite heart taking the lowest place; Barnes treats the opening verb as an idiom for setting about business and argues that the offended father is the only place left to go.
Wesley marks the accuracy of the steps and glosses heaven as God; Clarke grants the periphrasis but reports the rival rendering “even unto heaven”, an idiom for sinning beyond description.

Augustine asks whether the two clauses name one thing or two, offering the father’s supremacy, or the souls of the saints against the sanctuary of conscience; Ambrose reads the Spirit’s gifts or the heavenly Jerusalem, and urges that God waits for the voice of confession though he knows all things; Bede notes the request is pitched below sonship on purpose.
Chrysostom proposes that heaven here stands for Christ, since to sin against the visible heaven is to sin against the manhood he assumed.

debates: What “against heaven” means. Barnes and Wesley take it as the customary substitute for the name of God, while Clarke passes on a rendering that makes it an idiom of degree rather than an object; Chrysostom proposes Christ; Augustine offers the father’s supremacy or the souls of the saints; Ambrose the gifts of the Spirit or the heavenly Jerusalem.

19.pericope_label: I am no more worthy to be called thy son; make me as one of thy hired servants. And he arose and came, and when he was yet a great way off his father saw him, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck and kissed him

schools.summary: Gill takes the renunciation to cover national adoption and argues that the resolve proved to be of grace because it was executed, in another’s strength; Calvin argues from lesser to greater, that God will not be harsher than fathers prone to revenge, and attacks as sophistry the inference that grace waits upon a repentance men produce themselves.

Robertson calls the disclaimer a confession of the facts and finds in the genitive absolute a father already watching; Barnes lists humility, love of home and confidence in the request, adds that the son’s sense of his father was inadequate as every sinner’s is, contrasts a son who came slowly with a father who ran, and locates the point of the parable here; Ellicott dresses the returning man as poor in spirit, needing more than rags of his own.
Wesley notes the resolve was executed the moment it was made; Clarke presses the compound verb to mean he kissed him again and again.

Chrysostom reads the running as God coming to those who cannot reach him, and the kiss as given to the mouth that made the confession; Gregory of Nyssa says the meditated confession alone won the father over.

Ambrose has the father hear the heart’s secrets and run out lest anyone stop him, foreknowledge in the running and mercy in the embrace, and prefers being a son to being a sheep; Augustine makes the neck the place where the Father lowers his own Arm, which is Christ.

debates: Whether the father’s running proves that grace precedes repentance. Calvin sets the verse against opponents who argue that God shows grace only to those who first begin to seek him, granting that grief of conscience is required for pardon but denying that such repentance is a man’s own production; Gill argues the same way from the son’s rising, which he says was made and executed in another’s strength.

21.pericope_label: The son confesses that he has sinned and is no more worthy to be called a son; the father calls for the best robe, a ring and shoes

schools.summary: Calvin defines a second branch of repentance as conviction attended by grief and shame, distinguishes this confession from the auricular kind, and allows that the Father restores the gifts he had stripped away; Gill hears grace in the conjunction and has the son prevented from asking pardon by the kiss already given.

Ellicott hears an unvaried confession and a dropped request, since a man who has felt the kiss cannot ask for a hireling’s place; Robertson defends the disputed clause on manuscript grounds and reads the robe as first in rank, with ring and sandals as marks of a freeman; Barnes refuses to spiritualise the gifts at all, taking them as narrative colour for a single truth.

Clarke judges the extra clause an interpolation that spoils the beauty of an interrupted confession, and supplies the festal garment, the ring of dignity and the shoes restored with liberty; Wesley draws the moral that God often cuts an earnest confession short with a display of pardoning love.

Augustine has the son nobly disdain the request after the kiss, and makes the robe the dignity Adam lost and the servants the preachers of reconciliation; Ambrose calls the robe the cloak of wisdom and the ring the seal of unfeigned faith, and Bede reads the hand as a man’s working.

Chrysostom notes that the father answers the steward rather than the son, because a penitent receives no reply in words but sees mercy at work; Theophylact takes the servants for ministering spirits or for priests who clothe the soul with Christ in baptism.

debates: Whether the words “make me as one of thy hired servants” belong in the son’s speech. Clarke calls them an interpolation supplied to match the earlier resolve; Robertson notes the leading early manuscripts carry them and supposes the father broke in; Ellicott and Augustine hold that the son himself dropped the request once he had been kissed.

Whether the robe, ring and shoes should be read symbolically. Barnes forbids it outright and Calvin calls minute allegorising idle, while Ellicott, Ambrose, Augustine, Bede and Theophylact each assign the gifts a meaning.
outliers: Clarke supports the note on shoes with the price of Bengali and Chinese footwear in his own day.

23.pericope_label: Bring the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and be merry; for this my son was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found

schools.summary: Gill identifies the calf with Christ in allusion to the sin, peace and burnt offerings of the day of atonement, and unfolds the death as death in Adam, death under the law’s sentence, and death in trespasses and sins.

Ellicott takes the verb as the technical word for slaying a victim and finds a hint that the joy required a death, with the article pointing to a calf already fattened for a particular feast; Robertson denies the sacrificial sense outright and keeps to the vocabulary, an animal fed on wheat and kept for festive occasions; Barnes corrects the English “merry”, which suggests jovial mirth where the Greek means simply joy, and weighs two senses of “was dead”, preferring death to virtue.

Clarke renders the imperative “sacrifice it” and explains that feast animals were first offered to God, the flesh consecrated and the guests fed on divine food; Wesley insists the word rendered merry implies no levity but a solid, serious, heartfelt joy.

debates: Whether the calf is killed sacrificially. Clarke and Ellicott both press the sacrificial force of the verb, Clarke from ancient feast custom and Ellicott from its technical use, while Robertson denies it flatly and takes the killing as ordinary provision for a feast.
outliers: Clarke supports the sacrificial reading from present-day eastern custom rather than from the passage or its Jewish background.

25.pericope_label: Now his elder son was in the field, and as he came and drew nigh to the house he heard musick and dancing

schools.summary: Gill identifies the scribes and Pharisees by eliminating angels, mature converts and the Jewish nation; Calvin grants the national reading some force but holds it inattentive to the occasion, and notes that Christ concedes the boast for the sake of argument.
Henry takes the character for the Pharisees though not of them alone, and finds grace shining almost as bright in God’s bearing with peevish saints as in his receiving of prodigals.

Barnes takes the elder son for the Pharisees and defends the mention of dancing without endorsing it; Ellicott identifies a symphony of voices and instruments and derives our word choir from the second term; Robertson keeps the dance as a circular one on the green.
Clarke reports a scholar who denies the word means dancing at all, taking it for a choir of singers; Wesley identifies the elder son with the scribes and Pharisees of the opening verses.

Bede marks the third parable as the one that blames the envious; Augustine reads the elder son as Israel, out in the field of the Law and the Prophets, and takes the father’s going out as an open calling of the Jews after the fullness of the Gentiles; Ambrose makes the younger son the Gentile people and derives the elder’s age from envy; Jerome traces the kid to a deliverance from Rome that never came and adds that all human justice is injustice beside God’s.
Theophylact widens the figure to everyone offended at the sudden salvation of others.

debates: Whom the elder son represents. Barnes, Wesley and Gill confine him to the scribes and Pharisees, Gill arguing the point by eliminating angels, mature believers and the nation; Augustine and Ambrose read Israel against the Gentiles; Calvin grants that reading some argument but judges it inattentive to the occasion; Theophylact generalises to anyone who resents another’s salvation.

What the kid means. Ambrose reads it as the sacrifice the Jew still waits for and links it to Antichrist; Augustine rejects that reading with three objections and makes the kid the Lord himself, withheld from a nation that reckons him a sinner; Jerome makes it a deliverance from Rome; Theophylact a persecutor whose downfall would have given relief.

Whether “dancing” means dancing. Clarke reports a denial that the word ever means it, and Ellicott derives it from the dramatic chorus and includes song, while Robertson keeps a literal circular dance.
outliers: Barnes leaves the verse to argue at length about the propriety of dancing and what may or may not be pleaded from scriptural examples.

26.pericope_label: He calls a servant and asks what these things mean, and is told that his brother is come and his father has killed the fatted calf because he has received him safe and sound

schools.summary: Gill finds it characteristic that the son questions a servant rather than his father, as the scribes put their objections to a disciple rather than to Christ, and records the variation among the versions at the opening of the answer.

Robertson distinguishes the servant questioned from the bondslaves of the earlier verse, reads the imperfect as eager repeated inquiry, defends the indirect question against a charge of poor Greek, and works through three tenses in the report, ending with a father who has got his son back in good health despite everything; Ellicott gives the last word as literally “in health” and notes the participle as characteristic of Luke and Paul.
Wesley notices which detail the servant chose, guessing that the calf was mentioned rather than the robe or ring because it stood nearer to the music and dancing.
Augustine reads the consultation as the searching of a prophet, so that the question is why these feasts are kept in the church, and hears in the answer the new song rising from the end of the earth.

28.pericope_label: He is angry and will not go in; his father comes out and entreats him, and he answers that he has served many years and never transgressed, yet was never given a kid to make merry with his friends

schools.summary: Gill reads the offence as anger at the preaching of a crucified Christ and free, discriminating grace; Calvin grants the boast for argument’s sake and answers that not even a holiness equal to the angels would justify complaining that a brother is pardoned.

Robertson makes the anger an ingressive explosion after long resentment, sets the aorist of never transgressing against the present of long serving, and notes what the complaint avoids saying;  Ellicott presses the verb for slavish service and traces the absence of joy to an unconsciousness of transgression; Barnes calls the complaint unreasonable.

Clarke argues from the earlier division and from eastern inheritance law that the anger was groundless,; Wesley finds the resentment natural, identifies this son with the just persons of the earlier verse, and suggests God gives little joy to those who never felt the sorrows of repentance.

Augustine limits the unbroken commandment to the worship of one God, so that the son stands for Israelites who never turned to idols; Jerome likens him to the Pharisee justifying himself, keeping the law in the letter; Ambrose warns that grudging pardon to another may cost us our own.

Theophylact turns the concession into a question, whether being truly just could ever be a reason to refuse those who turn from iniquity; Chrysostom answers that no saint grieves at another’s good but counts it his own.

debates: Whether the elder son’s claim of unbroken obedience is to be believed. Wesley takes him for one of the just persons who need no repentance named earlier in the chapter; Ellicott and Robertson treat the claim as the Pharisees’ own valuation of themselves; Calvin and Theophylact concede it hypothetically only, to show that even a perfect obedience would give no right to resent a brother’s pardon; Augustine narrows it to a single commandment actually kept.
outliers: Clarke again settles the question of inheritance rights from an eastern law code rather than from Jewish practice.

30.pericope_label: But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf

schools.summary: Gill takes the refusal of the word brother as a refusal of the relation the father had just acknowledged, and reads the objection as offence that a crucified Christ should be preached to sinners so soon.

Barnes calls “this thy son” an expression of great contempt and a striking instance of petty malice, insulting brother and father at once; Robertson catches what is not said, neither “came back” nor “came home”, renders the verb for devouring as eaten down, and observes that the charge about harlots may be true but was beyond the accuser’s knowledge, and may show what he would have done himself; Ellicott hears a concentrated malignity in the turn of the phrase.
Clarke finds supreme contempt in a man who will not use his brother’s name, reproaching an affectionate father in the same breath.

Jerome likens the speaker to the Pharisee justifying himself, keeping the law in the letter while accusing his brother wickedly; Augustine reads the harlots as Gentile superstition; Ambrose warns that grudging pardon to another may cost a man his own.

outliers: Robertson notes that the accusation about harlots, though it matches the narrative, is something the speaker could not have known.

31.pericope_label: Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine

schools.summary: Calvin divides the answer into two arguments, that the brother’s reception costs the elder son nothing and that grief at another’s rescue is wicked hardness of heart; Gill grants the title of son by creation, national adoption and profession.

Robertson notes the informal “child” and the emphatic pronoun of a man who never appreciated his privileges at home; Ellicott raises and rejects the suggestion that the compliment is ironical, since the covenants, law and promises really had been given and only the power to use them was lacking; Barnes settles the legal question, that the property had been divided and what remained was already the elder son’s.

Wesley finds a strong reason against murmuring, since receiving the younger son disinherited nobody, but adds that the returning sinner will not be raised to a glory equal to that of those who have made greater progress in holiness.

debates: Whether the words are ironical. Ellicott raises the possibility that they are spoken from the Pharisees’ own point of view and rejects it, holding them literally true of Israel; Wesley turns them into a comparative reward, denying the penitent an equal glory where the servant has made greater progress; Calvin and Barnes take them as a plain statement that the elder son had lost nothing.

32.pericope_label: It was meet that we should make merry and be glad, for this thy brother was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found

schools.summary: Gill adds that the elder brother had reason of his own to keep the feast, had he felt for his kinsmen what the apostle felt for his.

Ellicott presses the Greek for moral necessity rather than fitness, finds the repeated “he was dead” singularly emphatic, and hears tenderness as well as reproof in the answer “this thy brother”; Robertson locates the necessity in the father’s heart, notes that the two verbs mean deep-seated joy and not hilarity, and ends with the objectors silenced by a picture of their own attitude.

Wesley calls the change of pronoun one of a thousand delicate touches an inattentive reader misses, and draws from it the intimation that the best of men should account the worst sinners their brethren still; Clarke has the father return his son’s unkind words in a wholly different spirit and holds that the hearers, unable to approve the elder son, had to condemn themselves in silence.

outliers: Clarke frames his closing reflections on the parable around a devotional writer’s three-part scheme rather than the text.
